occupancy.rationale: No official NJ ALR occupancy or vacancy dataset was located (see not_claimed), so these three values are operator planning assumptions, not sourced facts. New buildings ramp up from a small initial census, and the generator charges the ramp-up deficit. Rent and most staffing are fixed regardless of census, so results are sensitive to occupancy; the 85% case matters.

payroll_burden.notes: Payroll taxes 11% = employer FICA 7.65% (federal statutory rate, operator-applied) + NJ unemployment insurance for a new employer at 2.8% + employer temporary disability insurance 0.50% for new employers [S35]. The 2.8% new-employer rate is a combined figure: 2.6825% UI plus 0.1175% Workforce Development/Supplemental Workforce Fund (NJDOL Table C, FY2026-27, 7/1/2026 to 6/30/2027); the two figures seen in secondary sources are not in conflict [S33]. The 2026 UI taxable wage base is reported as $44,800 [S32], so nearly all aide wages are taxable. Federal unemployment tax (FUTA, typically 0.6% on the first $7,000 per employee after the state credit, about $42 per employee per year) is not itemized separately; treat it as absorbed in the 7% benefits estimate. No entity-level tax is modeled; have a CPA confirm the tax treatment. Workers' compensation 5% is an operator estimate (premium rates and class codes for residential care were not found; the $1,199 figure in [S32] is a benefit cap, not a premium). Benefits 7% is an operator estimate. All modeled wages are at or above the NJ minimum wage of $15.92/hour effective 1/1/2026 [S28]; the 2027 CPI-adjusted rate was not checked. No local minimum wage ordinance (Newark, Jersey City, etc.) was found.

configurations.label: 20-unit ALR, 90% private pay / 10% Medicaid (MLTSS)
configurations.notes: Smallest realistic apartment-style ALR in the model. CPCH is reported closed to new entrants [S51] (unverified), so a small residential-home model is not offered. The 10% Medicaid share reflects the rule that a newly licensed ALR must reach at least 10% Medicaid-eligible occupancy within three years, waivable by the Commissioner [S10]. At 90% occupancy (18 residents) this configuration loses about $2,900/month: fixed costs (rent, the 24/7 two-person staffing floor [S6], administrator) are spread over too few residents. It needs a rate above the CareScout median, a lower rent or owner-administrator labor to work. The CareScout $8,710 figure measures a private one-bedroom in an AL community [S27]. Medicaid revenue uses the SFY2026 base per diem [S16] (CMS approval unconfirmed), plus the resident room standard of $996.40 [S20]; whether a facility may collect that full amount from the resident is unverified.

configurations.label: 40-unit ALR, 90% private pay / 10% Medicaid (MLTSS)
configurations.notes: The configuration an expert operator would pick: large enough to spread the 24/7 staffing floor [S6] and administrator, with the 10% Medicaid share needed to satisfy the rule that new ALRs reach at least 10% Medicaid-eligible occupancy within three years (waivable) [S10]. At 90% occupancy (36 residents) it nets about $33,000/month on a revenue of about $295,800 before debt service and owner distributions, and needs roughly 76% occupancy to break even. Private pay uses the CareScout 2025 NJ median of $8,710 [S27], which measures a private one-bedroom in an AL community and fits apartment-style ALRs best. Medicaid revenue uses the SFY2026 base per diem [S16] (CMS approval unconfirmed) plus the resident room standard [S20]; whether the facility may collect the full $996.40 is unverified.

sections.executive_summary:
New Jersey licenses three assisted living categories through the NJ Department of Health (DOH) under N.J.A.C. 8:36 [S1][S14]. The **Assisted Living Residence (ALR)** offers apartment-style housing, dining and assisted living services. Each unit has at least one unfurnished room, a private bath, a kitchenette and a lockable entrance door [S1][S9]. The **Comprehensive Personal Care Home (CPCH)** is a room-and-board license with units of no more than two residents [S1][S14]. The **Assisted Living Program (ALP)** is a services-only license for residents of publicly subsidized housing [S9][S14]. A secondary guide reports that new CPCH licenses are not available, but this was not verified in rule text [S51]. This report therefore models the apartment-style ALR, the route a new entrant would realistically take.

A **Certificate of Need (CoN)** must come first. A license application can be filed only after a CoN is received [S2], and DOH's CoN table lists new assisted living facilities as eligible for expedited review [S13]. DOH's full-review long-term-care CoN instructions set a filing fee of $7,500 for a total project cost up to $1,000,000, and $7,500 plus 0.25% of total project cost above that (N.J.A.C. 8:33 Appendix B). The 40- and 60-unit builds exceed $1 million, so the fee is roughly $12,000 to $16,000 or more. Whether expedited review for new assisted living uses the same fee, and the review timeline, are not confirmed (see "What this report does not claim").

Most revenue is private pay. CareScout's 2025 survey puts the New Jersey median for an assisted living community at $104,520 a year, about $8,710 a month [S27]. The 2024 survey figure was $102,570, about $8,548 a month [S25]. Medicaid pays for care services only. Long-term care for assisted living runs through NJ FamilyCare managed care (MLTSS) [S49][S21]. DHS's FY2026 notice sets a base per diem of no less than $91.10 for ALRs, $81.10 for CPCHs and $79.10 for ALPs [S16]. These are SFY2026 rates; SFY2027 began July 1, 2026 and no SFY2027 rate notice was checked, so they may have been superseded. The resident pays room and board; the 2026 DMAHS ALR room standard is $996.40 a month [S20][S47]. The state notice said DHS would seek CMS approval of these rates, and no official post-approval source was found [S16]. On top of the base, P.L. 2023, c.80 adds tier per diems for ALRs and CPCHs with a higher Medicaid census: $10 at 15% to under 30%, $15 at 30% to under 50%, $30 at 50% to under 70% and $35 at 70% or more, measured as the yearly average from paid claims against total licensed beds [S17]. The model does not include these add-ons.

Licensing fees are small next to the rest of the budget: $1,500 plus $15 per bed, a $2,100 initial fee for 40 beds [S3]. The costs that decide the outcome are the CoN and construction work, rent, and the staffing floor of at least one awake personal care assistant plus one additional employee on premises at all times [S6]. Those staffing levels are minimums, and staffing must scale to resident acuity [S6]. N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2 also requires at least one registered professional nurse available at all times.

**Bottom line from the model (90% occupancy, default ramp, base per diem only):**
- **60-unit ALR, 90% private / 10% Medicaid:** nets about $71,900/month (16.2% margin). It breaks even at about 69.7% occupancy, first profit month is 12, and the model's total cash need is about $3.39 million.
- **40-unit ALR, same mix (the default):** nets about $32,900/month (11.1% margin). It breaks even at about 76.1% occupancy, first profit month is 11, and the cash need is about $2.25 million.
- **20-unit ALR:** loses about $2,900/month (-1.9% margin) and needs about 92.4% occupancy to break even.
- **40-unit, 30% Medicaid:** loses about $2,700/month (-1.0%) and needs about 91.4% occupancy at the base per diem. At 90% occupancy the census is about 27% of licensed beds, so the $10 tier add-on (unmodeled, about $3,300/month) would bring it to roughly break-even if it stacks on the base.
- **40-unit, 70% Medicaid:** loses about $73,900/month (-39.1%) at the base per diem. The $30 tier that a 63% census would earn (unmodeled, about $23,000/month) still leaves a loss of about $50,900. Even 100% occupancy does not break even at the base per diem.

These net and cash-need figures exclude the Medicaid tier add-ons, any cost for 24/7 RN availability, and the CoN filing fee line added after the runs (about $7,500 to $16,000), so they shift modestly.

In short, New Jersey assisted living works in this model at 40 units or more with a mostly private-pay census. A small building or a Medicaid-heavy census does not work at the published base per diem.

### What this report does not claim
- The CoN review timeline, whether expedited review uses the full-review filing fee, and DOH processing times for initial licensure or renewal.
- Whether CMS approved the FY2026 per diems, the post-approval effective date, and any SFY2027 rate change. MLTSS plan contract rates paid to individual ALRs are also not claimed, nor how the tier add-ons stack on the base.
- ALR Medicaid billing codes and units, and whether an ALR must join MLTSS. Secondary sources conflict [S50][S47].
- Statewide occupancy, competitor names, market shares, licensed-facility counts by type, and referral-source volumes. No official dataset was found.
- NJ-specific OEWS wages for RNs, administrators, cooks, housekeepers and recreation workers. Only the O*NET/BLS home health aide wage was retrieved [S30].
- The cost and exact meaning of 24/7 RN availability, the 2027 NJ minimum wage, insurance minimums, workers' compensation premiums, and local zoning standards. Premiums in the model are operator estimates.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** An ALR is licensed by DOH to provide apartment-style housing and congregate dining, with assisted living services when needed [S9][S14]. Residents are mostly private-pay older adults. Residents who qualify for MLTSS need a nursing-home level of care, shown by hands-on help with three or more activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing and mobility [S21].

**Licensing categories.**
- **ALR:** each apartment unit has at least one unfurnished room, a private bathroom, a kitchenette and a lockable entrance door [S1]. The applicant must apply for a license covering the maximum number of beds available in its residential units [S2].
- **CPCH:** a room-and-board license where residential units house no more than two residents [S1][S14]. A secondary guide estimates about 30 CPCHs statewide and says the category is closed to new entrants [S51]. Neither claim is confirmed against a DOH roster or rule text.
- **ALP:** an organization licensed to provide all services required of an assisted living program [S1]. ALPs serve tenants of publicly subsidized housing [S9]. They must deliver services exclusively in a licensed ALR, a CPCH or publicly subsidized housing [S11].

**Advertising.** Only licensed ALRs and CPCHs may describe and offer themselves to the public as providing assisted living [S12]. Do not market before you are licensed.

**Built-in commitments.** The license application must commit that at least 20% of residents will have nursing-home-level care needs within 36 months of licensure [S2]. A newly licensed ALR or CPCH must reach at least 10% Medicaid-eligible occupancy of its total bed complement within three years, subject to waiver by the Commissioner [S10]. Facilities adding beds after September 1, 2001 must also fill at least 10% of the added beds with Medicaid-eligible residents (same waiver) [S10]. These commitments shape the payer mix and the clinical staffing needed, which is why the model uses a 10% Medicaid share as its base case.

**Rule status.** N.J.A.C. 8:36 was readopted with technical changes and carries a new expiration in 2028 [S1]. DOH has said it is developing a broader revision and reorganization of the chapter [S1]. Its status is unknown. DOH also proposed (PRN 2026-003, 58 N.J.R. 1(1)) to let CPCHs use accreditation-based deemed status in place of a DOH inspection. The change would be optional, and comments were due March 6, 2026 [S7][S8]. Adoption has not been confirmed, and the change would not affect ALRs.
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Sequence.** The sequence below follows the rule text and DOH pages. The rules reviewed give no processing times, so no timeline is claimed.

1. **Form the entity and secure the site.** An LLC certificate of formation costs $100 on the Treasury schedule [S36], consistent with a CPA guide [S37]. Register for state taxes (a secondary guide says Form NJ-REG within about 60 days [S40]).
2. **Certificate of Need.** A license application may be filed only after a CoN is received [S2]. New assisted living facilities are listed as expedited-review eligible on DOH's CoN page [S13], and an HHS compendium also states that assisted living services require a CoN before licensure [S15]. DOH's full-review long-term-care instructions set a filing fee of $7,500 up to $1,000,000 of total project cost, or $7,500 plus 0.25% of total project cost above that; the fee must accompany the application or it will not be accepted (N.J.A.C. 8:33 Appendix B). Whether expedited review uses the same fee, and the review time, are not confirmed; call CN&L at 609-292-6552.
3. **Construction plan review.** For a new or expanded facility, plans go to DCA's Health Care Plan Review Unit for approval before construction starts [S1].
4. **Local approvals.** Before a license issues, you must file approvals from the local zoning, fire, health and building authorities, plus a certificate of occupancy [S1]. Local siting standards (distance, density, use class) were not found.
5. **License application.** File on DOH forms (https://www.nj.gov/health/forms) with proof of payment, by email to CNLapps@doh.nj.gov. Applications without proof of payment are not processed [S3][S1].
6. **Pre-opening survey.** DOH surveys on site once the written application is approved and the building is ready for occupancy [S1].
7. **Admissions.** No resident may be admitted until the facility has DOH's written approval or license [S1].

**Fees (nonrefundable) [S3][S2].**

| Item | Amount | When |
|---|---|---|
| CoN filing fee (full-review schedule) | $7,500, plus 0.25% of total project cost above $1,000,000 | With the CoN application |
| ALR/CPCH initial license | $1,500 + $15 per bed (40 beds = $2,100) | With the application |
| ALR/CPCH annual renewal | $1,500 + $15 per bed | Annually |
| ALR/CPCH biennial inspection | $1,500 | In the inspection year, together with that year's annual fee |
| ALP initial license / biennial inspection | $1,125 / $750 | Per DOH fee page |
| Transfer of ownership | $1,500 | Filed by the new owner before transfer |
| Relocation | $375 | Per N.J.A.C. 8:36-2.2 |

The application fee is capped by N.J.S.A. 26:2H-12 [S2]. License fee amounts were verified on DOH's fee page (last reviewed 2/11/2026) [S3] and on a Cornell mirror of the rule [S2]. The mirror is not the official code page.

**Administrator.** The administrator must be at least 21, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, and hold either a current NJ nursing home administrator license or a current NJ assisted living administrator certification [S4]. Certification candidates must sit the Assisted Living Competency Examination within two years of completing the training course [S4]. They must also complete a criminal background check, and the certificate runs three years [S5]. Renewal needs at least 30 hours of continuing education and a background check [S5]. A qualified owner may serve as administrator [S4]. Course hours and price were not verified. DOH's Certified Assisted Living Administrators office is at 609-633-9706.

**Medicaid enrollment.** The federal CY2026 provider enrollment application fee is $750 for applications filed in 2026 [S24]. Whether an ALR counts as an institutional provider for this fee was not confirmed, and no NJ-specific enrollment fee was found.

**Ownership changes.** A prospective new owner must file an application before the transfer takes place [S1]. A secondary guide says the license belongs to the operator, not the building, and is not transferable [S51].
sections.reimbursement:
**How the money flows.** New Jersey Medicaid long-term care for assisted living is delivered through NJ FamilyCare managed care (MLTSS), not a standalone fee-for-service benefit [S49]. The state's MLTSS guidance says MLTSS covers care in settings that include assisted living facilities [S21]. MLTSS pays for care services after the beneficiary enrolls in a managed care plan, and the resident pays room and board [S47]. A secondary source says the county welfare agency computes the resident's cost share and the facility bills and collects it [S48].

**Medicaid rates.**
- **Base per diem (SFY2026):** DHS/DMAHS gave notice that ALRs, CPCHs and ALPs would receive no less than $91.10, $81.10 and $79.10 per NJ FamilyCare beneficiary per day [S16]. The state-published SFY2026 rate list (posted by HCANJ) sets unlisted ALRs at $91.10, effective July 1, 2025 [S19].
- **Status caveat:** the notice says DHS would seek CMS approval, and no official post-approval source was found [S16]. SFY2027 began July 1, 2026; no SFY2027 rate notice was checked, so check njmmis.com ('rate and code information') and DMAHS legal notices. Treat $91.10 as an SFY2026 figure that may be superseded.
- **Statutory floor:** P.L. 2023, c.80 sets minimums of $89.50 (ALR), $79.50 (CPCH) and $89.50 (ALP) in the enacted text [S18]. The bill synopsis listed a different ALP figure, so verify [S18].
- **Medicaid-volume tiers:** ALRs and CPCHs receive a per diem above the minimum based on their yearly average Medicaid census, taken from paid claims and measured against total licensed beds: $10 at 15% to under 30%, $15 at 30% to under 50%, $30 at 50% to under 70%, and $35 at 70% or more. Below 15% there is no add-on [S17]. The FY2026 notice says the tier enhancements based on Medicaid volume are unchanged [S16]. How DMAHS stacks the add-on on the new $91.10 base is unconfirmed, so the model does not add any tier; confirm with DMAHS. At under 100% occupancy a nominal mix can land in a lower tier than its percentage suggests.
- **Codes and schedules:** procedure codes and billing units were not found. The state says fee schedules will be posted on its fiscal agent's website, njmmis.com [S16].
- **Budget neutrality:** the rate change is stated to stay within the 1115 waiver's budget-neutrality limits [S16].

**Resident contribution.** DMAHS's 2026 HCBS monthly standards for an ALR are $996.40 for room and $147.65 for maintenance (personal needs), effective January 1, 2026 [S20]. A secondary source puts the personal needs allowance near $140.15 [S48]. The official DMAHS figure is used. Whether a facility may collect the full $996.40 from the resident is unverified. The model counts it as revenue, so treat it as a risk to the Medicaid revenue line.

**Eligibility (2026).** The state's guidance sets a $2,000 resource limit and a $2,982 monthly income level, above which a Qualified Income Trust is needed [S21]. Clinical eligibility is a nursing-home level of care, with hands-on help for three or more ADLs [S21].

**Conflicts to resolve with DMAHS.**
- **ALR participation in MLTSS:** one secondary source says ALRs are not legally required to accept MLTSS residents [S50]. Another says the residence must participate [S47].
- **AL/AFC slot cap:** an undated secondary source reports a 1,500-slot cap and a full waiting list [S52]. Another describes MLTSS as an entitlement with no enrollment cap [S53]. The 2026 position is unverified.
- **Aged HCBS waiver:** a secondary source says New Jersey no longer offers an aged HCBS waiver and routes services through managed care [S53].

**Financing context.** NJ FamilyCare spending is $22.8 billion, 65% of it federal. State budget materials flag possible reductions in federal matching rates for high-income states like New Jersey. No enacted change was verified [S23].

**Private pay is the main payer.** CareScout's 2025 median is $104,520 a year (about $8,710 a month) [S27]. CareScout measures a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community, which fits an apartment-style ALR. It may not fit shared rooms or smaller homes. A secondary source reports about $8,234 a month, which does not match CareScout and is unreconciled [S47].
sections.demand:
**Demographics.** NJDOH reports that 18.0% of New Jersey residents were 65 or older in 2024, the same as the U.S. share. That proportion rose 33% between 2010 and 2024 [S45]. A secondary analysis citing Census data says the number of New Jerseyans 65 and over grew 43% over the same period [S46]. That is not a state-published count.

**Medicaid long-term care population.** The March 2026 NJ FamilyCare enrollment summary shows 305,056 aged, blind and disabled eligibles, 107,058 of them in the aged group, and 63,998 people in home and community-based waiver programs [S22]. Total NJ FamilyCare enrollment was 1,815,571 [S22]. The ABD figures describe the Medicaid long-term care pool. They do not count ALR residents.

**Supply context.** NJDOH licenses more than 2,000 regulated facilities of all types [S13]. No official roster by type or any ALR occupancy data was located. A commercial directory lists 887 New Jersey assisted living listings [Where Assisted Living, unofficial] and an editorial site analyzed 319 communities. Neither is an official count, so no supply or market-share figure is asserted.

**Payer-mix friction.** A Medicaid-planning law firm reports that most assisted living facilities require a private-pay period of two years or more before accepting Medicaid [S54]. This secondary source suggests many operators limit Medicaid admissions. For a new ALR, the 10% Medicaid-occupancy commitment is the countervailing rule [S10].

**Referral sources.** Hospital, nursing home and area agency referral volumes were not researched, and no waitlist figures were found. Build the referral plan from local hospital discharge planners, MLTSS plan care managers and county agencies, and test it before committing to a unit count.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.3).** The facility must keep at least one awake personal care assistant (PCA) on the premises at all times, plus one additional employee [S6]. A facility with more than one free-standing building with residents needs a PCA in each building [S6]. These levels are minimums only, and staffing must scale to resident acuity [S6]. In the model, the two-person floor is 1,460 hours a month, and acuity-scaled PCA hours are added at an operator estimate of 55 hours per resident-month. Numeric staff-to-resident ratios and overnight nursing rules beyond this section were not verified.

**Nursing coverage (N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2).** A facility must have at least one registered professional nurse available at all times, and each resident receives an RN assessment and care plan. The model's RN line covers only 80, 173 or 260 hours a month; no on-call stipend, relief or contract RN cost for the remaining hours is modeled. Confirm with DOH what 'available' means for coverage and response time.

**PCA qualifications.** A PCA must have completed an approved nurse aide course and passed the NJ Nurse Aide Certification Examination, or completed the approved PCA course and certification [S1]. Dementia training is required for all licensed and unlicensed direct-care staff if you advertise a dementia program [S1].

**Administrator.** The administrator needs an NJ nursing home administrator license or an NJ assisted living administrator certification [S4]. Renewal of the three-year certificate needs 30 hours of continuing education and a background check [S5]. Whether a full-time on-site administrator is required by bed count was not verified.

**Clinical oversight.** The 20% nursing-home-level commitment within 36 months [S2] and MLTSS eligibility (three or more ADLs) [S21] mean you need clinical leadership in practice. The model includes a director of nursing/RN at an operator-estimated wage and hours. No NJ RN wage was retrieved, so verify locally.

**Reporting and compliance.**
- Reportable events go to DOH immediately by telephone at (609) 633-9034, or (609) 392-2020 after hours. Written confirmation follows within 72 hours [S1].
- Report resident days for the prior calendar year by April 15 each year [S1].
- Apply before any transfer of ownership [S1].
- Keep local fire, health and building approvals current [S1].

**Systems.** The model includes eMAR and care documentation software. NJ EVV (HHAeXchange, the state-selected free vendor) is required by federal law for certain NJ FamilyCare services. Its go-live list names personal care and MLTSS home-based supportive care, and does not name ALR residential care [S41][S42]. Whether EVV applies to ALR-based MLTSS services is unconfirmed, so no EVV cost is modeled. Ask your MLTSS plans.

**Payroll obligations.** The NJ minimum wage is $15.92 an hour from January 1, 2026 [S28]. Every modeled wage is at or above it. NJDOL must publish a CPI-adjusted 2027 rate about September 30, 2026; that rate was not checked, and wages paid after January 1, 2027 must meet it. The 2026 unemployment taxable wage base is reported as $44,800 [S32]. The model's new-employer unemployment rate of 2.8% is the combined NJDOL Table C figure for FY2026-27: 2.6825% UI plus 0.1175% Workforce Development/Supplemental Workforce Fund [S33]. Employer TDI is reported at 0.50% for new employers [S35]. Federal unemployment tax (FUTA) is not itemized separately and is treated as absorbed in the benefits estimate.
sections.market_conditions:
**Private-pay pricing.** CareScout's NJ median for an assisted living community rose from $102,570 a year in 2024 ($8,548 a month) [S25] to $104,520 in 2025 ($8,710 a month) [S27], about 1.9%. The model uses the 2025 figure. Another source reports about $8,234 a month [S47]; it is unreconciled and below both CareScout figures. The model's sensitivity analysis shows what that price would do.

**Wages.** O*NET's New Jersey table, drawing on BLS 2025 wage data, shows home health and personal care aide hourly wages of $15.49 (10th percentile), $16.67 (25th), $17.83 (median), $21.43 (75th) and $23.16 (90th) [S30]. The 10th-percentile figure sits below the $15.92 minimum that took effect in 2026, because the data predates the increase [S28]. The same source's New York-Newark-Jersey City metro figures are $18.60 (25th), $19.08 (median) and $21.05 (75th) [S30]. The model uses the statewide figures: the awake PCA at the 75th percentile ($21.43), the additional employee at the median ($17.83), and housekeeping at the 25th percentile ($16.67), even though rent is benchmarked to the Newark area. A Newark-area site would pay more than modeled at the median and 25th percentile, and the additional-employee and housekeeping lines sit below the local 25th percentile; on the metro figures the 40-unit labor cost would be roughly $1,900 a month higher (approximate). Cook, housekeeping and activities wages are home health aide proxies, not their own occupations' wages. The BLS all-occupation mean wage in the New York-Newark-Jersey City area was $41.50 an hour in May 2025, which gives a sense of regional labor-market tightness [S31]. It is not an assisted living wage. No local minimum wage ordinance was found for Newark, Jersey City, Paterson or Trenton, so nothing here claims a higher local floor.

**Occupancy.** No NJ ALR occupancy figure is cited. The model's 85% / 90% / 95% scenarios are operator planning assumptions.

**Real estate.** The HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rent for the Newark HMFA (Essex, Morris, Sussex, Union) is $1,612 (studio), $1,822 (1BR), $2,205 (2BR), $2,761 (3BR) and $3,137 (4BR) [S43][S44]. The model uses the 1BR value per licensed unit, plus a $300 per unit monthly allowance for common-area and pass-through charges. That is a residential benchmark and excludes dining, kitchen, activity and office space. Whether Newark was part of HUD's May 2026 mid-year revisions is unconfirmed.

**Regulatory environment.** N.J.A.C. 8:36 carries a 2028 expiration, and a broader rewrite is described as pending [S1]. The CPCH deemed-status proposal is pending adoption and is optional [S7][S8]. The July 2025 per diem notice and the March 2026 enrollment figures show active state financing of MLTSS [S16][S22]. State budget materials also flag a risk from federal matching-rate reductions [S23].

**Entity costs.** New Jersey does not impose a franchise tax on LLCs, according to a secondary source, though corporation business tax may apply by election [S39]. The LLC annual report is reported at $75 a year [S38]. Neither is confirmed on an official page, and the model's entity-tax line is negligible.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the model is built.** Revenue per resident-month is the sum over each line of rate × units × payer share. For the default 40-unit configuration:
- 90% private pay at $8,710 [S27].
- 10% Medicaid at $996.40 in resident room payments [S20] plus $91.10 × 30.42 days in per diem [S16], about $3,768 per Medicaid resident-month. At 90% occupancy this census is about 9% of licensed beds, below the 15% tier threshold, so no tier add-on applies.
- That blends to about $8,216 per resident-month. At 36 residents (90% of 40 units) revenue is about $295,800 a month.

Costs are built from the staffing rules and from operator estimates for items without a source. Rent is sized to licensed units: 40 units × $1,822 [S43][S44] plus $300 per unit in common-area allowance is $84,880 a month, fixed. Payroll burden is 23% (11% taxes, 5% workers' compensation, 7% benefits). The 11% is 7.65% employer FICA + 2.8% new-employer unemployment (2.6825% UI + 0.1175% WFD/SWF) [S33] + 0.5% TDI [S35]; workers' compensation and benefits are operator estimates, and FUTA is not itemized separately.

**Where the 40-unit default lands (90%, 36 residents).** The model's net is about $32,900 a month (11.1% margin). Using the modeled lines, the main cost blocks are:
- Payroll including burden: about $131,000 a month, 44% of revenue.
- Fixed operating costs, led by rent and the common-area allowance: about $100,700.
- Per-resident costs (food, supplies, insurance, activities, referral fees): about $30,800.

The staffing floor of 1,460 awake hours is paid whether 10 or 40 residents live there, so fixed costs absorb small census swings.

**Results by configuration (90% occupancy, base per diem, no tier add-ons).**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash need |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60-unit, 90/10 private/Medicaid | $71,913 | 16.2% | 69.7% | 12 | $3,386,022 |
| 40-unit, 90/10 | $32,871 | 11.1% | 76.1% | 11 | $2,254,510 |
| 40-unit, 70/30 | -$2,714 | -1.0% | 91.4% | none | $2,520,632 |
| 20-unit, 90/10 | -$2,852 | -1.9% | 92.4% | none | $1,118,639 |
| 40-unit, 30/70 | -$73,884 | -39.1% | 152.7% | none | $4,666,398 |

**Sensitivities (approximate, derived from the modeled lines).**
- **Occupancy:** each additional resident adds about $5,900 a month of contribution in the 40-unit default (revenue less per-resident costs and acuity hours). That puts the net at about $21,000 at 85% occupancy and about $9,200 at 80%. Break-even is 76.1%, so the 40-unit model works only if census holds.
- **Acuity hours:** the 55 hours per resident-month is an operator estimate. At 70 hours, the 40-unit net falls by about $14,200 to about $18,600. For the 20-unit it falls by about $7,100, deepening its loss to about $10,000 a month.
- **Private-pay rate:** every $100 on the private rate is about $3,240 a month at 32.4 private residents. At the unreconciled $8,234 [S47], the 40-unit net would be about $17,400. A rate near $7,700 would erase the profit.
- **Wages:** a 10% rise in all modeled wages costs about $13,100 a month, leaving the 40-unit net at about $19,700. The modeled wages are statewide benchmarks; the Newark-area metro aide wages ($18.60 / $19.08 / $21.05 at the 25th percentile, median and 75th) would raise the 40-unit labor cost by roughly $1,900 a month [S30]. No local minimum wage above the state's was found.
- **RN coverage:** a 24/7 RN availability cost (on-call stipend or contract RN) is required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2 but is not modeled; any such cost comes straight off the net, hitting the 20-unit model hardest.
- **Rent:** a 10% change in the $84,880 rent and common-area line is about $8,500 a month. Real commercial or purpose-built terms may differ materially from the HUD benchmark.

**Medicaid mix.** Each Medicaid resident brings about $4,940 less per month than a private-pay resident at base rates. Moving from 10% to 30% Medicaid takes the 40-unit net from +$32,900 to about -$2,700 at the base per diem only. The statutory tier add-ons are not in these figures. The census is the yearly average from paid claims measured against total licensed beds [S17]. At 90% occupancy a nominal 30% mix is about 10.8 Medicaid residents, or 27% of 40 licensed beds, which falls in the $10 tier. That would add about $3,300 a month ($10 × 30.42 days × 10.8) and bring the 30% model to roughly break-even, assuming the add-on stacks on the $91.10 base (unconfirmed with DMAHS). Without any tier, the per diem would need to be about $8 a day higher (about $99) to break even at 30% Medicaid. A nominal 70% mix at 90% occupancy is about 25.2 residents, or 63% of licensed beds, so the $30 tier would apply, not the $35 tier; the $35 tier needs 28 Medicaid residents (70% of 40 beds), i.e. a full building at a 70% mix. The $30 add-on would add about $23,000 a month and shrink the modeled loss of about $73,900 to about $50,900, so the tier does not rescue the 70% model. The 70% model also assumes private-pay-level staffing, although MLTSS residents need a nursing-home level of care [S21]. Actual MLTSS plan contract rates are unknown.

**Path to profit.** The configuration that works is 40 or more units, a mostly private-pay census held near the 10% Medicaid commitment [S10], full occupancy ramped within a year, and rent below or near the HUD benchmark. The 60-unit model shows better fixed-cost leverage (break-even about 69.7%) but needs about $3.39 million in cash, and a slower fill hurts more in absolute dollars.

**Honesty notes.** Most operating costs, the RN and administrator salaries, the acuity hours, workers' compensation and rent are operator estimates, not sourced facts. Occupancy, ramp and Medicaid room-payment collection are also assumptions. The net figures are before debt service and owner distributions, and exclude the Medicaid tier add-ons and any 24/7 RN availability cost. The cash-need figures include startup costs and the modeled ramp-up deficit, and the startup ranges are wide; they were computed before the CoN filing fee line (about $7,500 to $16,000) was added.
sections.risks:
**Rate and payer risk.**
- **Unconfirmed rates:** the $91.10 / $81.10 / $79.10 base per diems are SFY2026 figures that depend on CMS approval, which no official post-approval source confirms [S16]. SFY2027 began July 1, 2026 and no SFY2027 rate notice was checked, so the base may have changed. The state notice describes the increase as within the 1115 waiver's budget-neutrality limits [S16].
- **Tier add-ons:** the statutory Medicaid-volume tiers ($10 to $35 per day by census against licensed beds) are not modeled, and how they stack on the new base is unconfirmed [S17]. They are upside for Medicaid-heavy mixes, and a census below 100% of licensed beds can land in a lower tier than the nominal mix suggests.
- **Plan contracts:** MLTSS plan contract rates, terms and ALR participation rules are not researched [S50][S47]. Billing codes are unknown.
- **Room payment:** whether you may collect the $996.40 room standard from the resident is unverified [S20][S48]. The personal needs allowance (official $147.65 vs about $140.15 reported elsewhere) is unresolved [S48].
- **Federal funding:** state budget materials flag possible reductions in federal Medicaid matching for high-income states [S23]. No enacted change was verified.
- **Slot cap:** a reported AL/AFC slot cap and waitlist conflict with entitlement descriptions [S52][S53].

**Licensing and timing risk.**
- **CoN:** the CoN is a hard prerequisite [S2]. The full-review filing fee is $7,500 plus 0.25% of total project cost above $1 million, but the expedited-review fee and review time are unconfirmed, so a slow CoN adds carrying cost for any lease you have already signed.
- **Licensing steps:** DOH timing is not in the rule text reviewed. No admissions are allowed before written approval or license, and plan review, local approvals and the pre-opening survey all sit in the critical path [S1].
- **Rule changes:** N.J.A.C. 8:36 expires in 2028 and a broader rewrite is described as pending [S1]. The CPCH deemed-status proposal has an uncertain status [S7][S8].
- **Commitments:** the 20% nursing-home-level and 10% Medicaid-occupancy commitments affect staffing cost and payer mix [S2][S10].
- **Non-transferable license:** a change in ownership requires a new application before transfer and, per a secondary guide, voids the old license until approved [S1][S51]. This affects exit planning.

**Operating and financial risk.**
- **Fixed-cost leverage:** the two-person 24/7 staffing floor [S6], rent and the administrator are fixed. The 20-unit model loses money and the 40-unit default needs about 76% occupancy to break even.
- **Staffing:** minimums are floors only, and acuity may demand more than the modeled 55 hours per resident-month [S6]. See the financial narrative for the 70-hour result.
- **RN coverage:** N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2 requires a registered professional nurse available at all times. The modeled RN hours do not cover 24/7, and no on-call or contract RN cost is included, so true costs are higher than modeled.
- **Wages:** statewide benchmarks understate costs for a Newark-area site, where metro aide wages are higher at the median and 25th percentile [S30]. No local ordinance above the $15.92 statewide minimum was found [S28], and the 2027 state minimum was not checked.
- **Unverified costs:** insurance minimums, workers' compensation premiums, 24/7 RN coverage and the CoN consultant and construction costs are operator estimates or unmodeled.
- **Capital:** the model's cash need is $1.1 million to $4.7 million depending on configuration. A slow ramp raises it.
- **Private-pay price:** the CareScout median measures a private one-bedroom in an assisted living community [S27]. A lower local market price, or the $8,234 secondary figure [S47], reduces profit quickly.

**Market risk.** No occupancy, competitor or referral data were found. Many operators reportedly delay Medicaid admissions [S54], so assume you will compete for the same private-pay residents.
sections.recommendations:
1. **Choose the apartment-style ALR and plan at 40 or more units.** In the model, the 40-unit ALR is the smallest profitable configuration: about $32,900 a month at 90% occupancy, with break-even at 76.1%. A 60-unit building improves margin to about 16.2% and break-even to 69.7%, but needs about $3.39 million in total cash. Do not enter with 20 units unless owner labor (for example the owner serving as administrator, which removes a modeled $75,000 salary) and lower rent make the economics work. Even then, the 20-unit model is only slightly profitable at best, and it does not yet carry a 24/7 RN availability cost.

2. **Keep Medicaid near the required 10% and avoid heavy Medicaid.** The 10% commitment within three years [S10] is built into the default. At the base per diem the 30% Medicaid model loses about $2,700 a month; the $10 tier add-on it would likely earn (about $3,300 a month, unmodeled) would bring it to roughly break-even if confirmed [S17]. The 70% model loses about $73,900 at base and still about $50,900 with the $30 tier its census would likely earn. Revisit a larger Medicaid share only if MLTSS plan contracts pay materially more than the $91.10 base, and verify the plan rates and how DMAHS stacks the tier add-on first.

3. **Treat the CoN as the first gate.** Confirm the CoN filing fee (full-review schedule: $7,500 plus 0.25% of project cost above $1 million), whether expedited review [S13] uses it, and the timeline directly with DOH (CN&L, 609-292-6552) before committing to a lease or purchase. Do not sign a lease whose rent starts before you have a realistic path to licensure.

4. **Negotiate rent against the benchmark.** Rent plus common-area charges are about 29% of revenue in the default. The Newark 1BR FMR of $1,822 [S43][S44] is a residential benchmark. Obtain real commercial or purpose-built quotes, and test a 10% increase (about $8,500 a month).

5. **Hire a certified administrator early.** The administrator needs an NJ nursing home administrator license or assisted living administrator certification [S4][S5]. If you are the owner, you can serve if you qualify. Budget time for the training course, exam and background check.

6. **Staff above the floor, price the acuity.** The two-person floor [S6] is only a minimum, and N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2 also requires an RN available at all times. Model acuity hours and RN coverage realistically, and set your private-pay price to cover them. Do not set rates by copying the CareScout median alone.

7. **Protect the ramp.** Build the referral pipeline (hospital discharge planners, MLTSS care managers, county agencies) before opening, and plan cash for the model's ramp deficit. First profit is month 11 for the 40-unit default and month 12 for the 60-unit under the assumed fill pace.

8. **Resolve the open questions with DMAHS and DOH before you commit capital.** These are: MLTSS participation requirements, plan rates, any SFY2027 per diem change, how the tier add-ons stack on the base, whether you may collect $996.40 from residents, billing codes, the personal needs allowance, whether EVV applies, what RN 'available at all times' requires, insurance requirements, and rule changes under PRN 2026-003 and the rewrite.

9. **Stress-test before you invest.** Run your own numbers at 80% and 85% occupancy, 70 acuity hours, a lower private rate, Newark-area wages and wages 10% higher, and an added RN coverage cost. The default is profitable but sensitive to each.

checklist.task: Choose your license type: Assisted Living Residence (ALR), Comprehensive Personal Care Home (CPCH) or Assisted Living Program (ALP)
checklist.instructions: ALR = apartment-style housing, dining and assisted living services. CPCH = room and board; units house no more than 2 residents. ALP = meals and assisted living services to residents of publicly subsidized housing, delivered only inside a licensed ALR, CPCH or subsidized housing. A secondary source says CPCH licensing is closed to new entrants (unverified), so this bundle models the ALR. Confirm availability with the DOH Certificate of Need and Licensing Program before committing to any other type.

checklist.task: Select your size and payer mix using the Pro Forma P&L
checklist.instructions: In the model the 40-unit and 60-unit ALRs at 90% private pay / 10% Medicaid are profitable at default occupancy (about $32,900 and $71,900 net per month; break-even occupancy about 76% and 70%). The 20-unit ALR and the 30%/70% Medicaid mixes lose money at the SFY2026 base per diem. Do not raise rates or drop required costs to force a profit. Adjust rent, wages and census in the xlsx for your own site.

checklist.task: Read N.J.A.C. 8:36 in full and note its status
checklist.instructions: The chapter was readopted with technical changes and carries a new expiration date in 2028. DOH has said it is developing a major revision and reorganization of the chapter; no current status was found. Download the official text from DOH, since the Cornell LII mirror used in this research may lag. Re-check for changes before filing.

checklist.task: Check the pending 2026 amendment on CPCH deemed status (PRN 2026-003)
checklist.instructions: DOH proposed (58 N.J.R. 1(1), Jan. 5, 2026) to let CPCHs use accreditation-based deemed status in place of a DOH staff inspection, as an option only. Comments were due March 6, 2026. Adoption status was not confirmed. Look up the New Jersey Register for the current status.

checklist.task: Form your New Jersey LLC (or other entity)
checklist.instructions: File a certificate of formation with the Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services. The Treasury fee schedule lists $125; a CPA guide reports $100 effective 7/1/2026. Check the DORES portal for the fee in effect on your filing date. The licensee on the DOH application should match this entity exactly. Allow about a week.

checklist.task: Structure ownership around the fact that the license belongs to the operator, not the building
checklist.instructions: A secondary guide says an ALR license is issued to the operator, is not transferable, and a change of ownership voids it until DOH approves. Put the licensed operating entity on the application and lease. Keep the real-estate holding entity (if separate) in a written lease with the operator. Have a NJ health-care attorney review the structure.

checklist.task: Obtain an EIN
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov. It is issued the same day online. You need it for payroll, banking, state tax registration and Medicaid enrollment.

checklist.task: Register the business for NJ tax purposes (Form NJ-REG)
checklist.instructions: A secondary guide says registration is generally due within about 60 days of forming the LLC, using Form NJ-REG. Register for withholding, unemployment (UI) and TDI/FLI as an employer before your first payroll. Confirm the deadline with NJ Division of Taxation.

checklist.task: Calendar the LLC annual report and understand entity-level tax
checklist.instructions: A secondary guide gives a $75 annual report fee due the last day of the month in which the LLC was formed. The official page fetched did not show this fee, so verify it. Secondary sources say NJ does not impose a franchise tax on LLCs, though corporation business tax may apply if you elect it. Ask your CPA. The model carries $75 per year and no entity tax.

checklist.task: Open a business bank account and secure start-up capital
checklist.instructions: Capitalize for the whole pre-opening period and ramp-up. The model's cash need through ramp-up is about $1.1M (20 units), $2.25M (40 units) and $3.39M (60 units). It includes build-out, CON preparation, pre-opening payroll and operating deficits. These are operator-estimate-based model outputs. No state-mandated minimum reserve was found.

checklist.task: Engage a NJ health-care attorney and CON/licensing consultant
checklist.instructions: CON, DCA plan review, local approvals and MLTSS participation all interact. Budget is an operator estimate; the model uses $15,000–$40,000 for CON preparation. Interview at least two firms that have filed NJ long-term-care CONs.

checklist.task: Obtain insurance quotes (general/professional liability, property, auto, workers' compensation)
checklist.instructions: No liability or bond minimum for ALR licensure was found, but landlords, lenders and MLTSS plans typically require coverage. Workers' compensation premium rates and class codes for residential care were not found (the $1,199 figure is a benefit cap, not a premium). The model's premiums are operator estimates. Get written quotes before signing a lease.

checklist.task: Confirm the Certificate of Need (CON) pathway for a new ALR
checklist.instructions: A license application may be filed only after a certificate of need has been received. DOH's CoN table lists new assisted living facilities as eligible for expedited review. Call the CoN and Licensing Program at (609) 292-6552 (verify current) and ask for the current application form, fee and review timeline. This research could not confirm the fee or timeline from official sources.

checklist.task: Do not sign a binding lease, start construction or advertise before the CON is in hand
checklist.instructions: The licensing sequence is CON first, then license application to the Commissioner, then survey, then admissions. Negotiate lease contingencies tied to CON approval, zoning and licensure so you are not paying rent on a building you cannot license.

checklist.task: Prepare and file the CON application
checklist.instructions: Use the forms DOH prescribes (check https://www.nj.gov/health/forms and the CoN page). Typical contents are a need/market analysis, financial feasibility, site and building description and ownership disclosure. Confirm the exact list with DOH. Fee and timeline unverified; do not assume the figures quoted in secondary sources.

checklist.task: Build the demand case with sourced data
checklist.instructions: NJDOH reports 18.0% of NJ residents are 65+ (2024, same as the U.S.), up 33% as a share between 2010 and 2024. A secondary source reports the count grew 43%. No official occupancy, waitlist or ALR supply count was found. Do not cite competitor shares or occupancy without a source. Use CareScout's 2025 NJ median of $8,710/month (private one-bedroom in an AL community) as a pricing benchmark and caveat it.

checklist.task: Plan for the 20% nursing-home-level-of-care commitment
checklist.instructions: The application must commit that within 36 months after licensure at least 20 percent of residents will have nursing-home-level care needs. This drives staffing, RN oversight and admission criteria. Budget acuity-based hours above the staffing floor (the model uses 55 PCA hours per resident-month, an operator estimate).

checklist.task: Plan for the Medicaid-eligible occupancy requirement
checklist.instructions: A newly licensed ALR/CPCH must attain Medicaid-eligible occupancy of at least 10 percent of its bed complement within three years (waivable by the Commissioner). ALRs/CPCHs adding beds after Sept. 1, 2001 must occupy at least 10 percent of the additional beds with Medicaid-eligible persons. Ask DOH whether a waiver applies to your project.

checklist.task: Apply for the maximum number of beds the building can hold
checklist.instructions: The rule requires the facility to apply for a license for the maximum number of beds available in its residential units. Size your unit count and the fee ($1,500 + $15 per bed) from that number. Fixed costs in the model are sized to licensed units, so choose carefully.

checklist.task: Design units to meet the minimum unit standard
checklist.instructions: ALR apartment units must offer, at a minimum, one unfurnished room, a private bathroom, a kitchenette and a lockable door on the unit entrance. CPCH units house no more than two residents and have a lockable entrance door. Have your architect confirm every unit type against the current rule text.

checklist.task: Shortlist sites and benchmark rent
checklist.instructions: HUD FY2026 Fair Market Rent for the Newark HMFA (Essex, Morris, Sussex, Union) is $1,612 (0BR), $1,822 (1BR), $2,205 (2BR). The model uses $1,822 per licensed unit plus a $300/unit common-area/CAM allowance. This is a residential benchmark only and excludes dining, kitchen, activity and office space. Get real broker quotes; other NJ regions may be cheaper.

checklist.task: Obtain local zoning approval
checklist.instructions: The license application must include approvals from the local zoning authority. Local siting standards (distance, density, use class) were not found. Meet the municipal zoning officer early and ask whether the use is permitted, conditional or needs a variance. Allow time for board hearings (timing varies by town).

checklist.task: Submit construction plans to DCA Health Care Plan Review before building
checklist.instructions: Plans for a new or expanded facility must go to the NJ Department of Community Affairs Health Care Plan Review Unit for review and approval before construction starts. Budget architect/engineering of $25,000–$150,000 (operator estimate) and plan-review time before the build-out schedule.

checklist.task: Obtain local fire, health and building approvals
checklist.instructions: Approvals from the local fire, health and building authorities are required before licensure. Ask the fire official what alarm, sprinkler and egress systems apply to your building. Model allowances for fire alarm monitoring and inspections are operator estimates.

checklist.task: Obtain the certificate of occupancy
checklist.instructions: File the certificate of occupancy with the license application. Schedule final building inspections so the CO is issued before you ask DOH to survey.

checklist.task: Negotiate the lease with licensing contingencies
checklist.instructions: Vacant units still cost rent, so the model treats rent as fixed. Negotiate free-rent months during build-out, a tenant-improvement allowance, a contingency on CON/DCA/DOH approvals, landlord consent to the use and a lease term that covers the ramp-up. Have counsel review it.

checklist.task: Budget the build-out and equipment
checklist.instructions: Model ranges (operator estimates, get contractor quotes): unit build-out $300,000–$1,200,000; commercial kitchen/dining/common areas $40,000–$120,000; furnishings and resident-care equipment $60,000–$180,000; zoning/fire/health/building approvals and CO $5,000–$25,000.

checklist.task: If you have more than one free-standing resident building, plan staffing per building
checklist.instructions: Any facility with more than one free-standing building with residents must provide at least one personal care assistant on the premises at all times in each building. This multiplies the 24/7 staffing floor, so treat it as a site-selection factor.

checklist.task: Download current DOH license forms
checklist.instructions: Forms are on the DOH forms page (https://www.nj.gov/health/forms) and through the Certificate of Need and Licensing Program. Use the current ALR initial-license application.

checklist.task: File the license application after receiving the CON
checklist.instructions: The operator applies to the Commissioner for a license on forms prescribed by the Department. Applications are filed after the CON is received. Include the CON, local zoning, fire, health and building approvals and certificate of occupancy, and the 20% nursing-home-level commitment.

checklist.task: Pay the initial ALR/CPCH license fee and send proof of payment
checklist.instructions: The fee is $1,500 + $15 per bed, nonrefundable (20 beds $1,800; 40 beds $2,100; 60 beds $2,400). It is paid with the application. DOH will not process an application without proof of payment. Pay through the DOH long-term care fee page and email the documents and proof of payment to CNLapps@doh.nj.gov.

checklist.task: Confirm when the $1,500 biennial inspection fee is due
checklist.instructions: The fee schedule lists a $1,500 biennial inspection fee. The rule says it is assessed in the year the facility will be inspected, along with that year's annual licensure fee. Ask DOH whether it is charged in your initial licensure year. The start-up budget includes it as a precaution.

checklist.task: Prepare your policies and procedures, resident agreement and admission/retention criteria before the survey
checklist.instructions: DOH will survey for compliance with N.J.A.C. 8:36. Write policies for each subchapter. Align admission and retention criteria with your CON commitments (20% nursing-home-level residents; Medicaid-eligible occupancy). Have counsel review the resident agreement. Content must be checked against the current rule text.

checklist.task: Budget time for DOH review
checklist.instructions: No rule-quoted processing timeline for initial licensure was located. Ask the program for current turnaround, and do not sign hires or marketing commitments that assume a fixed date. Application fees are nonrefundable, so file only when the package is complete.

checklist.task: If you plan an Assisted Living Program (ALP) license, note the separate fees and service location rule
checklist.instructions: ALP initial licensure fee is $1,125 and biennial inspection fee is $750. ALP services must be provided exclusively in a licensed ALR, CPCH or units of publicly subsidized housing. ALP staffing and eligibility details under 8:36-23 were not fully verified.

checklist.task: Secure a qualified administrator
checklist.instructions: The administrator must be at least 21, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, and hold either a current NJ nursing home administrator license or a current NJ assisted living administrator certification. A qualified owner may serve as administrator. Whether a full-time on-site administrator is required by bed count was not verified; ask DOH.

checklist.task: If certifying a new administrator, complete the training course, exam and background check
checklist.instructions: Candidates must sit for the Assisted Living Competency Examination within two years of completing the assisted living training course, and must complete a criminal background check. Course hours and price were not verified (the model budgets $1,000–$3,000 as an operator estimate). Contact the DOH certification unit for current providers.

checklist.task: Build the 24/7 staffing floor
checklist.instructions: At least one awake personal care assistant plus one additional employee must be on the premises at all times. The model costs 730 hours per month for each. The levels are minimums only; you must staff to resident acuity. Numeric ratios and overnight nursing rules beyond 8:36-9.3 were not verified, so confirm with DOH.

checklist.task: Add acuity-based hours above the floor
checklist.instructions: The model adds 55 PCA hours per resident-month (operator estimate; verify locally). Medicaid MLTSS residents must need nursing-home level of care (hands-on help with 3+ ADLs), so a higher Medicaid share likely means more hours than modeled. Test a worse value (for example 70 hours) in the xlsx.

checklist.task: Verify PCA qualifications for every aide
checklist.instructions: A PCA must have completed an approved nurse aide course and passed the NJ Nurse Aide Certification Examination, or completed the approved PCA course and certification. Collect proof of certification at hire and keep it in the personnel file.

checklist.task: Hire clinical oversight (RN / director of nursing)
checklist.instructions: RN and nursing minimums in the current rule were not verified, but the 20% nursing-home-level commitment makes clinical oversight a practical necessity. The model uses an operator-estimate $50/hour (80 hrs/month for 20 units, 173 hrs for 40, 260 for 60). Ask DOH what nursing coverage your license requires.

checklist.task: Set wages at or above the NJ minimum wage
checklist.instructions: The NJ minimum wage is $15.92/hour effective 1/1/2026 (from $15.49). O*NET/BLS 2025 NJ home health aide wages: 10th percentile $15.49, 25th $16.67, median $17.83, 75th $21.43, 90th $23.16. No local minimum wage ordinance was found, but check your municipality. A secondary source reports $15.23 for employers with fewer than six employees; do not rely on it for a facility this size.

checklist.task: Set up payroll taxes and workers' compensation
checklist.instructions: The model uses 11% payroll taxes: FICA 7.65%, NJ UI for new employers 2.8% combined (disputed; another source says 2.6825%), and employer TDI 0.50% for new employers. The 2026 UI taxable wage base is reported as $44,800. Confirm all rates on your NJDOL registration and rate notice. Workers' compensation (5% modeled, operator estimate) needs a carrier quote.

checklist.task: Run background and registry screening on all staff
checklist.instructions: Background-check requirements for owners and direct-care staff beyond the administrator were not verified in this research. Ask DOH and your counsel what is required, and run screening on every hire before first shift.

checklist.task: Train all direct-care staff in dementia care if you advertise a dementia program
checklist.instructions: Facilities advertising a dementia program must train all licensed and unlicensed staff who provide direct care to residents with dementia. Document the curriculum, dates and attendance. If you do not advertise a dementia program, still plan dementia-aware training because of acuity.

checklist.task: Set private-pay pricing from sourced benchmarks
checklist.instructions: CareScout's 2025 NJ median for an assisted living community is $104,520/yr (about $8,710/month); the 2024 survey median was $102,570/yr (about $8,548/month). CareScout measures a private one-bedroom in an AL community. A secondary source reports about $8,234/month and does not reconcile. Verify pricing against competing communities within your catchment area.

checklist.task: Implement an eMAR / care documentation system
checklist.instructions: The model carries $15 per licensed unit per month (operator estimate). Choose software that supports service plans, medication administration records and incident reports. Get vendor quotes.

checklist.task: Set up a reportable-events procedure
checklist.instructions: Reportable events must be phoned to DOH immediately at (609) 633-9034 (or (609) 392-2020 after hours), with written confirmation within 72 hours. Post the numbers at the nurses' station and train every shift lead.

checklist.task: Set up resident-day tracking for the annual DOH report
checklist.instructions: Facilities report resident days for the prior calendar year to the licensing program by April 15 each year. Build the count into your census software from day one.

checklist.task: Set up dietary service and food vendor
checklist.instructions: ALRs provide congregate dining. The model uses about $450 per resident per month for food (about $14.80 per resident-day; operator estimate). Get vendor quotes and confirm kitchen requirements with the local health authority.

checklist.task: Contract for fire-alarm monitoring, sprinkler/alarm inspections and extinguisher service
checklist.instructions: Model allowance: $400–$900 per month by size (operator estimate). Get vendor quotes and align with what the local fire official requires.

checklist.task: Contract accounting, payroll service and legal support
checklist.instructions: Model allowance: $1,500–$3,500 per month by size (operator estimate). Set up monthly census-based financials so you can track the break-even occupancy in the P&L.

checklist.task: Decide whether and how you will participate in MLTSS, and confirm with DMAHS
checklist.instructions: NJ Medicaid assisted living care services are delivered through NJ FamilyCare managed long-term services and supports (MLTSS). Secondary sources conflict on whether an ALR must participate (one says not legally required; another says it must). Ask DMAHS in writing. Remember the 10% Medicaid-eligible occupancy requirement under 8:36-5.1.

checklist.task: Understand how MLTSS money flows
checklist.instructions: MLTSS plans pay for care services in a participating residence after the beneficiary enrolls in an NJ FamilyCare managed care plan. Medicaid does not pay room and board; the resident does. MLTSS settings include assisted living facilities. Plan-specific contract rates and terms were not researched; get them from each plan.

checklist.task: Use the state's published per diems as a floor in your projections
checklist.instructions: DHS notice (7/16/2025): base per diem of no less than $91.10 (ALR), $81.10 (CPCH), $79.10 (ALP) per beneficiary per day, with tier add-ons unchanged. A state rate list posted by HCANJ shows $91.10 for unlisted ALRs effective 7/1/2025. CMS approval and any FY2027 changes were not confirmed. Fee schedules are to be published on njmmis.com.

checklist.task: Understand the high-Medicaid tier
checklist.instructions: Under P.L. 2023, c.80, ALRs and CPCHs with a 70% or more Medicaid census receive a per diem $35 higher than the minimum per diem, measured yearly from paid claims. How DMAHS applies the add-on to the $91.10 base is unconfirmed. Do not budget the add-on until you have it in writing.

checklist.task: Learn MLTSS eligibility rules for prospective residents
checklist.instructions: Applicants need nursing-home level of care (hands-on assistance with three or more ADLs), $2,000 or less in total resources, and income at or below $2,982/month in 2026, or a Qualified Income Trust if higher. Train admissions staff to screen early and to refer families to the county welfare agency or a benefits specialist.

checklist.task: Set up room-and-board billing for Medicaid residents
checklist.instructions: DMAHS 2026 HCBS standards for an ALR resident: room $996.40/month and maintenance (personal needs) $147.65/month, effective 1/1/2026. A secondary source gives about $140.15 for the personal needs figure, so use the DMAHS number and verify. A secondary source says the county computes the cost share and the facility bills and collects it. Confirm how much you may collect before relying on $996.40 in pricing.

checklist.task: Check the Medicaid provider enrollment application fee
checklist.instructions: CMS set a $750 application fee for institutional providers, required with enrollment applications submitted on or after 1/1/2026 (calendar 2026). Whether an ALR is classed as an institutional provider, and any NJ-specific enrollment fee, were not confirmed. Ask DMAHS and the plans.

checklist.task: Ask your MLTSS plans whether EVV applies to your services
checklist.instructions: NJ's EVV (HHAeXchange, state-selected free vendor) is required for certain NJ FamilyCare services. The go-live list names personal care and MLTSS home-based supportive care and does not name ALR residential care. Congregate settings are exempt per a DDD letter. Whether EVV applies to ALR-based MLTSS services is unconfirmed, so get the answer in writing.

checklist.task: Plan the Medicaid ramp conservatively
checklist.instructions: A secondary source says most ALFs require a long private-pay period before accepting Medicaid, and a separate undated source reports a capped AL/AFC slot program. Neither is verified for 2026. Model shows heavy-Medicaid mixes (30% and 70%) lose money at the base per diem, so do not rely on Medicaid to fill a new building.

checklist.task: Request the DOH pre-opening survey
checklist.instructions: DOH conducts an on-site survey when the written application for licensure is approved and the building is ready for occupancy. Have staff hired and oriented, policies in place, systems working and the building complete before the survey. Correct any deficiencies promptly.

checklist.task: Do not admit any resident before you hold written DOH approval or a license
checklist.instructions: No facility may admit residents until it has the written approval or license from DOH. Keep a pre-admission waitlist only; no move-ins until you have the document in hand.

checklist.task: Follow the advertising restriction
checklist.instructions: Only facilities licensed as assisted living residences or comprehensive personal care homes may describe and offer themselves to the public as providing assisted living services. Do not use the term in marketing materials until you are licensed. Review the website and brochures with counsel.

checklist.task: Build referral relationships
checklist.instructions: Cultivate hospital discharge planners, skilled nursing facilities, elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers and area agencies on aging. Referral-source volumes were not found in official data, so build your pipeline from direct outreach. The model amortizes $150 per private-pay resident per month for placement fees (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Plan a phased fill and monitor cash
checklist.instructions: The model starts with 3–6 residents and adds 2–4 per month depending on size; the 40-unit default first turns a monthly profit in about month 11 and 60 units in month 12. Track census weekly against the break-even occupancy in the P&L (about 76% for 40 units, about 70% for 60 units).

checklist.task: Run a pre-opening open house and launch marketing after licensure
checklist.instructions: Model range for launch marketing: $10,000–$50,000 (operator estimate). Use only licensed-status language, and include your license number in materials if DOH issues one.

checklist.task: Pay the annual license renewal
checklist.instructions: Renewal is $1,500 + $15 per bed each year, nonrefundable (40 beds = $2,100). Pay it on the DOH long-term care fee page and send proof of payment by email. The model carries it as a monthly accrual.

checklist.task: Budget the biennial inspection fee
checklist.instructions: The $1,500 biennial inspection fee is assessed in the year the facility will be inspected, along with that year's annual licensure fee. Keep the building survey-ready at all times.

checklist.task: File the annual resident-days report by April 15
checklist.instructions: Report resident days for the prior calendar year to the licensing program by April 15 each year. Pull the data from your census system in March.

checklist.task: Renew the administrator certificate every three years
checklist.instructions: Certificates run three years. Renewal requires at least 30 hours of continuing education on assisted living concepts and related topics, and a background check. Track the expiration date and book CE well in advance.

checklist.task: Keep staffing at or above the floor and the acuity level
checklist.instructions: At least one awake PCA plus one additional employee on premises at all times; levels are minimums only. Review staffing against resident acuity monthly and after any incident.

checklist.task: Track progress toward the 20% and 10% commitments
checklist.instructions: Within 36 months of licensure, at least 20% of residents must have nursing-home-level needs, and the facility must reach at least 10% Medicaid-eligible occupancy (waivable). Document admissions and acuity so you can show compliance at survey.

checklist.task: File a change-of-ownership application before any transfer
checklist.instructions: Before transferring ownership, the prospective new owner must submit an application to the licensing program. The rule fee is $1,500 for a transfer of ownership and $375 for relocation (nonrefundable). Do not close on a sale or transfer entity interests without DOH sign-off.

checklist.task: Monitor rule and rate changes
checklist.instructions: Watch for adoption of the 8:36 rewrite and the CPCH deemed-status amendment, the 2028 expiration of the chapter, FY2027 per diem changes, CMS approval status of the $91.10 base, and the pending personal-needs-allowance bill (A2691/S1576, status reported only by a secondary source). The state budget materials also flag possible federal match reductions for high-income states.

checklist.task: File the LLC annual report and keep state tax registrations current
checklist.instructions: The LLC annual report ($75 per a secondary guide; verify) is due by the last day of the month in which the LLC was formed. Keep NJDOL UI/TDI filings current and update rates when each year's notice is issued.

checklist.task: Review the P&L each quarter against the model
checklist.instructions: Compare actual census, payer mix, wages and rent to the pro forma. Rent and most staffing are fixed regardless of census, so a few vacant units move results quickly. Re-run the break-even occupancy before adding Medicaid beds or changing staffing levels.
